assumptionsReview.context: Library-side body drain when parser returns undefined (FR-014; api.md §2)
assumptionsReview.choice: After every parser call, library checks `if (!part.body.destroyed && part.body.readable)` and drains via `for await (const _chunk of part.body) {}`. No-op when parser already drained. Without this, dicer's per-part Readable buffers indefinitely; the closing boundary doesn't make it through; truncation detector mis-fires. Discovered during first test run (T-006/T-007 failed with MultipartTruncatedError before the drain was added).
assumptionsReview.rationale: Verified at src/fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts:251-265 by Read. Honors api.md §2 explicit contract: 'parser returning undefined skips the part; the part body is drained internally before the next yield'. Layer A's parseMultipartRelated cannot perform this drain because it is consumer-agnostic (it cannot know whether the consumer's parser drained or not — Layer A drains in cleanup() for the iterator-`break` path, but not between yields). The for-await drain idiom is canonical for a Node Readable; uses the same `for await` machinery the consumer would use, no race with dicer's next 'part' emission. T-007 (parser always returns undefined → parts.length === 0) verifies this empirically — without the drain, this test would reject with MultipartTruncatedError. The eslint-disable for the `_chunk` unused variable is necessary and correctly scoped.

assumptionsReview.context: wrappedOnProgress shape — should bytes always be tracked even when caller doesn't supply onProgress?
assumptionsReview.choice: Layer B always supplies an INTERNAL `onProgressForLayerA` to parseMultipartRelated regardless of caller. The internal callback unconditionally captures `lastBytes = snap.bytes`; when the caller supplied options.onProgress, the callback also forwards the snapshot. Layer A's fireProgress wraps THIS wrapper in try/catch + logger.warn — so caller's throw goes through Layer A's catch site (canonical). No double-log because Layer B doesn't catch in onProgressForLayerA.
assumptionsReview.rationale: Verified at src/fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts:166-171 — the inner closure captures lastBytes regardless of options.onProgress presence. This is correct: result.bytes always reflects the actual source bytes count (T-074 asserts result.bytes > 0 for happy-path; T-007 asserts result.bytes > 0 even when parser returns undefined). The architecture decision (no Layer B catch around forwarding) avoids double-log when caller's onProgress throws — Layer A's fireProgress catches and routes through the same logger. Verified by T-031..T-033 (events.length >= 3 — exactly per-part count, NOT 2x per-part). The completion-tick site at line 271-287 has its own catch (single-log) because Layer A doesn't fire that site.

assumptionsReview.choice: Preserved with the fetchAndHandleMultipart marker retired and the file's purpose-comment updated. The remaining 2 tests assert both public exports exist as functions — cheap regression guard against accidental drop of a re-export from src/index.ts.
assumptionsReview.rationale: Verified by Read of tests/integration/sprint-1-stubs.test.ts — file has 2 tests, BOTH are real (parseMultipartRelated returns AsyncGenerator + fetchAndHandleMultipart returns a Promise). The brief explicitly allows this file to be either modified-with-real-tests OR deleted; the generator's choice to preserve it as a smoke regression guard is consistent with the export-existence pattern. The test-count delta from Sprint 4 (3→2) reflects this retirement correctly.

assumptionsReview.context: fetch caller-signal forwarding — `fetch(url, { ...options.fetchInit, signal: options.signal })` overwrites any potential nested fetchInit.signal with options.signal
assumptionsReview.choice: Init is built as `{ ...(options.fetchInit ?? {}), ...(options.signal !== undefined ? { signal: options.signal } : {}) }` so when both fetchInit.signal AND options.signal are present, options.signal overwrites (defensive). The runtime FR-024 check at top of function should have already rejected if fetchInit.signal was set, so this overwrite is defensive belt-and-suspenders.
